claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates during controlled aging.
Nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by nanoscale precipitates enhances toughness.
Overaging causes precipitate coarsening.
Overaging promotes grain-boundary embrittlement that reduces toughness.
The proposed initial material is an as-cast high-entropy alloy with a predominantly single-phase, homogeneous microstructure and potentially metastable configurations.
Aging time at a selected temperature such as 450°C is the controlled variable proposed to alter precipitate evolution.
The proposed aging window is 400–500°C for 1–24 hours in an inert atmosphere.
The relevant structural mediator is precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction in the matrix and along grain boundaries.
Initial aging forms fine, uniformly dispersed precipitates within the matrix.
Extended aging causes precipitate coarsening and may promote segregation to grain boundaries.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, aging for approximately 4–8 hours is predicted to increase fracture toughness.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, aging for approximately 4–8 hours is predicted to increase ductility.
Aging for approximately 16–24 hours is predicted to reduce toughness in association with coarser precipitates and greater grain-boundary embrittlement.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to high-entropy alloys that begin with predominantly single-phase microstructures and undergo moderate aging.
The hypothesis may not apply to alloys containing substantial secondary phases or exposed to extreme aging temperatures or very long aging times.
The optimum aging time and temperature may vary with alloy composition.
Precipitate formation and growth kinetics may depend on subtle compositional and processing changes.
Failure of intermediate aging to improve toughness relative to the as-cast baseline would falsify the proposed hypothesis.

A lack of correlation between precipitate size or uniformity and toughness, or a lack of toughness decline accompanying coarsening and grain-boundary segregation during extended aging, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
